title: Legal Tech Insights: Sheppard Mullin's Legora selection and AI roadmap
author: Legal IT Insider

dom.t: Legora partnerships: Adoption needs selected workflows and training

st.t: Legora partnerships: Adoption needs selected workflows and training
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between acquiring Legora and achieving effective adoption. Cain presents Legora as an addition to an existing AI toolkit and argues that value depends on overcoming limited awareness and uneven use so that isolated successes become consistent firmwide practice. It does not provide independent evidence of productivity, accuracy or client outcomes.
qs: But not enough people knew about it, not enough people were using it, not enough people were getting value out of it.
We want to make that consistent across the organization.

kp.k: Client interest and maturing technology prompted evaluation
kp.d: Kate Cain says increasing client interest in suitable generative-AI projects, combined with the firm’s judgment that the technology had matured sufficiently, prompted Sheppard Mullin to evaluate legal AI assistants in 2025. This was an expansion of an existing AI strategy: the firm had previously adopted CoCounsel before Thomson Reuters acquired Casetext.
qs: Earlier this year, we were starting to hear from more and more clients expressing an interest in the kinds of projects that Legora and tools like it are really well suited for and decided that the technology itself had matured enough that it made sense for us to take a look at.
An early adopter of CoCounsel back in its pre-Thomson Reuters Casetext days, Sheppard Mullin is not a stranger to GenAI technology and has been keeping an eye on the legal AI assistant market

kp.d: The firm ran a two-vendor, head-to-head selection process from August to mid-October 2025. Eight partners, associate counterparts, transactional-training leadership, a diligence team, and the knowledge and innovation team tested both platforms through weekly cohort meetings and vendor office hours. Cain characterizes the result as close, with Legora judged the best organizational fit.
qs: Sheppard Mullin ran an intensive two-horse, head-to-head process led by eight partners.

Each partner had an associate buddy and the selection team also included the head of legal training for Sheppard Mullin’s transactional practices, a dedicated diligence team, and Cain’s knowledge and innovation team, who all worked with both platforms.
So we kicked that off in August, ran through the course of it, and by mid-October, we had made our decision that Legora was the best fit for us
Cain describes the outcomes as “a really close race”

kp.k: Nuance, validation, and support differentiated Legora
kp.d: According to Cain’s account of the pilot, users preferred Legora because its language appeared more nuanced and sophisticated, its validation functions increased confidence, and the vendor offered stronger training, support, implementation planning, and collateral. These are internal user assessments rather than independent benchmark results.
qs: Firstly, users found the language to be more nuanced and sophisticated.
Secondly, the validation gave them more confidence.
The third thing that jumped out was the training, support, implementation planning framework and resources from Legora
They came to us with really great collateral.

kp.d: Cain identifies verification as a central condition for responsible lawyer use because lawyers remain concerned about whether generative-AI output is correct, coherent, and relevant. Legora’s one-click access to source information and its explanations of drafting rationales were seen as helping lawyers check outputs and understand system behavior, rather than rely on outputs without review.
qs: That’s the part that keeps lawyers nervous about using generative AI: how do we make sure that it’s correct and coherent and relevant?
And so we want to make sure that any platform we put in front of our lawyers has really, really solid validation functionality so that they can check things with confidence.
The thing that stood out to us from Legora was that it was one click to be able to see what the source information was
Legora would give you the example language or the recommended language, but then it would explain its rationale, it would explain the analysis.

kp.d: Cain presents visible drafting rationales as both a verification aid and a training opportunity. In her view, explanations can help associates learn the analysis behind recommendations while allowing the firm to assess whether the application behaves as expected; the document provides no measured evidence yet of training outcomes.
qs: That that stood out for us because we could understand and become more confident that the application was behaving the way we would want it to and also, because we see that as a terrific training opportunity as associates start to be introduced to the platform.

kp.d: Sheppard Mullin plans to deploy Legora across every practice group and office for more than 1,200 attorneys. Intended applications include research, diligence, drafting, negotiation, and trend analysis, supported by practice-specific playbooks and continuing certification for attorneys and business-services professionals.
qs: Sheppard Mullin is rolling out Legora across all practice groups and offices, enabling more than 1,200 attorneys to use it for the likes of research and diligence, drafting and negotiations, and analysing trends.
The firm is creating practice-specific playbooks and ongoing certification to ensure attorneys and business services professionals are getting the most from it.

kp.k: Early transactional uses focus on contracts
kp.d: Reported early use cases include analyzing transactional markups, rewriting provisions toward a client’s preferred seller or buyer position, and answering targeted questions across sets of contracts. Cain distinguishes this “ad hoc diligence” from formal M&A due diligence and reports that the tool was especially useful for rapid, issue-specific contract review.
qs: Cain says that some of the early use cases revolve around analysing markups in transactional departments and rewriting provisions to be more in line with their client (pro-seller or pro-buyer, for example.)
Where we have found a lot of utility is in what I would refer to as ‘ad hoc diligence’

So not the official formal due diligence for an M&A, but more of a, ‘hey, take a look at this set of contracts and quickly identify where there are certain issues or whether X, Y, Z, circumstance will be an issue’.
If we take a look at these more ad hoc questions, it was really powerful

kp.k: Prior work product can scaffold new diligence
kp.d: In one internal project, a team supplied an earlier diligence report, related work product, and a new document set, then asked Legora to reproduce the desired tabular review format. Cain says the result was imperfect but close and could jump-start the task by generating prompts and a table from prior work product. This is an anecdotal project result, not a systematic evaluation.
qs: a team gave an old diligence report and work product together with a new set of diligence documents to Legora and said ‘create a tabular review that is going to look like this.’
And it did!
It wasn’t perfect but it was really, really close.
It drafted all of those prompts and that table based on the work product we fed it, which was pretty cool.

kp.k: AI may shift lawyers toward higher-value analysis
kp.d: Cain argues that the principal opportunity is augmentation: reducing time spent locating, collecting, and organizing information so lawyers can devote more effort to detailed analysis, matter strategy, and nuanced work requiring legal expertise and experience. The article does not quantify time savings or claim demonstrated changes to staffing, leverage, or pricing.
qs: Cain says that the really powerful opportunity for lawyers is less time hunting and gathering and organising and more time analysing and digging into the details and doing the strategy of matters
the more nuanced stuff that requires lawyers’ expertise and knowledge and experience and the things they went to law school for.

kp.k: Adoption outcomes remain too early to assess
kp.d: The agreement was executed in November 2025, so Cain says meaningful adoption evidence was not yet available. An initial lesson is that generative AI is not conventional button-driven software: effective use is iterative and requires lawyers, including partners, to learn how to formulate instructions, prompts, and workflows.
qs: Sheppard Mullin executed the agreement with Legora in November and it’s too soon to talk about adoption
one of the early learnings is that this isn’t software that you learn what the button does and push it, it’s far more iterative.
There is a learning curve for partners in terms of how to interact with and instruct Legora
We need to think through what the instruction is and that’s about building those prompts and workflows.

kp.k: Instruction should resemble supervising junior lawyers
kp.d: Cain recommends that partners formulate AI instructions by considering what context and direction they would give a summer associate. This frames prompting as a supervisory and workflow-design skill rather than a simple command, while retaining the lawyer’s role in specifying the work.
qs: If you were to give the same instruction to a summer associate, would you just say, ‘give me X?’ What would you tell them?’

kp.k: Rollout combines baseline and practice-specific training
kp.d: The implementation plan has two concurrent tracks: a firmwide introductory launch for baseline access and training, and more advanced practice- or team-specific deployments. Each practice group will use a discovery process to identify two or three initial workflows, templates, or applications that can be available from the first day of its rollout.
qs: The way we’re approaching the rollout is two concurrent rollouts.
One is a firm-wide launch. So a 101: everybody who wants in the pool can get in the pool. We’ll give everybody that baseline training and start to build up those muscles and that awareness.
At the same time, we’ll do practice-specific and team-specific rollouts where that’s the sort of 200 level, 300 level to use an American university analogy.

For each of those practice groups we’ve got a whole discovery process where we’re identifying what are the two or three starting workflows or templates or applications or things that we want to have at the ready for day one for those practice rollouts.

kp.k: Ethics and responsible use are continuous guardrails
kp.d: The firm plans to embed responsible AI use throughout training and communications, working with its office of general counsel to incorporate it into lawyers’ ethics and compliance training. Cain emphasizes client-centered, appropriate, and effective service, describing governance as an ongoing theme rather than a one-time disclaimer or compliance formality.
qs: We work really closely with our office of general counsel to make sure this is all incorporated into the ethics training and compliance training that all lawyers are part of.

Our general counsel team is fantastic and do a really great job of centering ethical, responsible use around the client and ensuring that we’re serving the client appropriately and effectively and really making it quite real for our lawyers.

So, it’s not just like a disclaimer that pops up or a disclaimer at the beginning of a training, it’s something that we talk about in lots of different channels so that it’s not a check the box kind of exercise.

kp.k: Innovation team prioritizes work transformation over deployment
kp.d: Cain describes the firm’s knowledge and innovation function as integrating innovation into practice groups and business-services teams. Its practice innovation team combines legal, knowledge, innovation, and technology expertise, represents lawyers during software evaluations, and aims to change working methods rather than merely deliver technology.
qs: A big piece of that remit is how do we look at innovation as a strategic priority for the firm, and how do we interweave it into everything that we do at the practice level, with the business service teams and such?
Cain is building out the practice innovation team – a group of knowledge and innovation attorneys who have technology expertise and can help to ‘be the voice of lawyers’ in software evaluations.
The goal for us is not to deliver software
The goal for us is to help our lawyers transform the way they work today and tomorrow.

kp.k: Existing tools suffered awareness and utilization gaps
kp.d: Cain reports that the firm had already invested in strong software, including AI-enabled tools, but insufficient awareness and use limited realized value. The innovation team has therefore emphasized communicating concrete matter-level successes to stimulate lawyer demand and diffuse adoption across the organization.
qs: What we learned very quickly as a team was that the firm has invested in some terrific software over the years. But not enough people knew about it, not enough people were using it, not enough people were getting value out of it.
Just raising awareness around AI-enabled tools that were already in the firm’s toolkit and making better use of them, raising awareness around them, highlighting wins is really valuable.
We’ll say, ‘Look, we used this for this particular real estate deal and here’s how it made an impact.’
Now I’ve got folks showing up in the doorways of my K&I attorneys saying, ‘Can I have what they were having?’

kp.k: Legora extends rather than begins AI strategy
kp.d: Cain positions Legora as one component of a pre-existing technology portfolio and a multi-year innovation roadmap. The strategic objective is to convert localized successes into consistent, institutionalized practices across the firm, although the document reports plans and anecdotal wins rather than organization-wide measured outcomes.
qs: I want to be clear, Legora isn’t the start. Legora is an addition to an existing toolkit.
We’ve already had wins across the firm. Our goal now is to institutionalize that.
We’ve had pockets of successes. We want to make that consistent across the organization.
And I think Legora is the next chapter of that journey.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Cain says legal AI assistants can accelerate preliminary diligence and drafting, with the larger opportunity being to redirect lawyers from information gathering and organisation toward analysis and strategy.
pts.d: Kate Cain, Sheppard Mullin’s chief knowledge and innovation officer, reports utility in analysing transactional markups, rewriting provisions to favour a client's position, and identifying issues across sets of contracts. She distinguishes the reported 'ad hoc diligence' from formal M&A due diligence. In one project, Legora used an earlier diligence report and work product to generate prompts and a tabular review for new documents. Cain describes this as an imperfect but useful starting point, not autonomous completion of legal work. Her broader claim about reallocating lawyers’ time is framed as an opportunity rather than a measured firm-wide outcome.

pts.k: Cain claims accessible source material and explanations of drafting recommendations support lawyers’ verification and confidence, and could help train associates.
pts.d: Cain identifies nuanced language, verification-supporting functionality, and implementation support as differentiators in the firm's selection of Legora. She says one-click access to source information and explanations of proposed drafting changes helped lawyers understand the application's behaviour. The associate-training benefit is an anticipated opportunity. These claims concern human review and understanding of AI output, not demonstrated accuracy rates or replacement of lawyer verification.

pts.k: Cain presents AI-enabled changes in legal work as dependent on iterative instruction, tailored workflows, organisational support and greater use of existing tools—not simply software acquisition.
pts.d: Cain reports that partners face a learning curve in instructing Legora and that existing firm software had been underused. She says raising awareness and publicising specific successes has stimulated interest in AI-enabled tools. The firm's intended next step is to turn isolated successes into consistent use across the organisation through baseline training, practice-specific workflows, certification, a practice innovation team and ongoing responsible-use training.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of Cain’s account of an internal comparative pilot, early work examples and implementation experience.
pts.d: Legal IT Insider reports a head-to-head evaluation of two platforms involving eight partners, each paired with an associate, alongside transactional legal training, diligence, and knowledge and innovation personnel. Both platforms were used, with weekly cohort meetings and vendor office hours. Cain characterises the result as close and Legora as the best fit for this firm. The diligence-table example and reports of interest in existing tools are qualitative internal experiences. The article supplies no numerical accuracy, time-saving, adoption, cost or client-outcome results, and no independent benchmark. The predicted benefits for strategic work and associate training are not accompanied by measured outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account concerns a 2025 selection and early rollout; broad adoption and sustained benefits remain prospective at publication.
pts.d: Published on December 4, 2025, the article dates the pilot from August to mid-October 2025 and the agreement to November. Cain says growing client interest and her assessment of technological maturity prompted the evaluation earlier that year. The article explicitly states that it is too soon to discuss adoption. Broader benefits are conditional on lawyers learning iterative prompting, having suitable workflows and templates, checking output, and receiving continuing training and support. The simultaneous firm-wide and practice-specific rollouts are implementation plans, not evidence of achieved firm-wide transformation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern a large law firm's lawyers, business services professionals and clients, with early applications concentrated in transactional work.
pts.d: Legal IT Insider reports a rollout across Sheppard Mullin’s practices and offices, enabling more than 1,200 attorneys to use Legora. Partners must learn how to instruct the tool; associates may gain a training aid from explained drafting recommendations; transactional teams gain assistance with markups, provisions and preliminary contract review. Business services professionals are included in the playbook and certification effort. Knowledge and innovation attorneys support tool evaluation and changes in working practices, while the firm's own general counsel team supports ethical and compliant use. Clients are described as expressing interest and as the intended beneficiaries of effective, responsible service, but the source does not report quantified client savings or changes to pricing, staffing levels or access to justice.
